answer.rationale:
The competitor price cut creates strong pull toward promotional_pricing, and memory_73 appears to endorse it. But the recovered source record exp_73 shows that consolidation is lossy in a value-relevant way: the discount cohort delivered +31% signups and +18% qualified revenue while 30-day retention fell 12%, and the source explicitly instructs against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. Against the stated objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue), matching the discount would buy a cohort that does not survive first renewal and would deepen the churn problem it is meant to solve. I therefore treat memory_73 as contaminated and exclude it, and I flag that any downstream agent inheriting memory_73 alone would likely make the wrong call.

The only direction with a corroborated source record is shortened onboarding: exp_86 confirms +13% completion, -2.1 days time-to-value, and +3% 30-day retention. That is the rare option that plausibly addresses the actual churn mechanism — price sensitivity is partly a value-realization problem, and faster time-to-value strengthens the retention side rather than trading it away. It is also the only claim I can currently stand behind on verified evidence.

The remaining memories (memory_31 signup simplification, memory_91 activation messaging, memory_57 referrals, memory_44 enterprise sales-assist) are unverified consolidations of the same type that failed for memory_73, so I do not treat them as load-bearing; they are the priority verification queue next week. Because my verification budget is spent and the competitor shock means current conditions differ from those under which exp_86 was run, I scope this as a standard experiment with retention and qualified-revenue instrumentation rather than a broad rollout, so the result is measurable and reversible. I am not claiming this fully offsets the competitive pressure — it may not, and that residual uncertainty should be carried forward rather than resolved by assertion.
